newsitem.title: HONG KONG: WEEK AHEAD - Hong Kong seen bucking dull Asian trend.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Hong Kong seen bucking dull Asian trend.

text.p: Asian stocks are poised for a lacklustre week with Hong Kong, once again, offering the only excitement.
The volatile Hang Seng index could rally further following a see-saw week, which saw blue chips plunge more than 900 points on local and Chinese factors, before a 1.35-percent recovery on Friday.
In Tokyo, sharp moves by the U.S. dollar-yen will play a major role, with stocks expecting a boost from pension fund allocations.
But the rest of the region is expected to remain stuck in a dull phase of sideways trade.

The markets will also keep a close eye on Wall Street after the Dow Industrials ended Friday 70.57 points, or 0.92 percent higher at 7782.04. It was the blue chip gauge's sixth-consecutive record closing high.
TOKYO - Tokyo stocks are seen range-bound this week ahead of the Denver Group of Seven summit, with attention trained on currencies, brokers said.

The yen yo-yoed wildly following the announcement that Japan's April current account surplus had jumped 92.7 percent from the previous year, which raised concerns over Japan's trade surplus ahead of the G7 summit meeting.
Brokers added that the supply-demand situation was likely to be robust, aided by pension fund allocations, with the market's downside likely solid at the 20,000 level.

"There is speculation that a vast amount of funds will come to the market via trust banks and investment trusts," said Katsuhiko Kodama, general manager at Toyo Securities. Market sources see a range of 20,150 to 20,800 for the key Nikkei 225 average in this week.
On Friday, the benchmark finished 36.11 points or 0.18 percent lower at 20,528.35 after climbing to hit a new 1997 year high of 20,815.48.
HONG KONG - Share prices should recover in the coming week after suffering their sharpest weekly slide in three months last week pulling them down to oversold levels, analysts said.
The Hang Seng Index tumbled 542.58 points last week, or 3.7 percent, to close at 14,112.55 on Friday. The blue chip index hit an intra-day low of 13,795.96 on Friday before rebounding.
"The market should improve next week after it rebounded from technical support at 13,800 on Friday," said Ricky Tam, senior research manager at Delta Asia Securities.
Monday's launch of a new China-play index, the 32-company Hang Seng China-Affiliated Corporations Index, should boost interest in the red chip sector, analysts said.
"It is going to maintain the interest and activity in the red chip stocks but with a stronger institutional bias," said Howard Gorges, vice chairman at South China Holdings.
"Quite a lot of fund managers will want to own stocks in those red chips," he said.
Gorges forecast the Hang Seng blue chip index will trade between 14,000 and 14,500 points this coming week and said the China-Affiliated Corporates Index could be quite volatile.
TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices are expected to consolidate next week with views divided on the market's short-term outlook after Saturday's big gain, brokers said.
Brokers said the market would largely depend on trend-setter shares in electronics.

"The market still sees electronics as the bellwether stocks that will lead its next bull run," said Yungli Securities analyst Chen Han-chung. "Investors will feel sort of insecure unless electronics finish their corrections."

On Saturday, the index closed 187.16 points or 2.25 percent higher at a two-month high of 8,502.18, up from 8,367.46 a week earlier. Brokers did not rule out the possibility that the index may fall below 8,500 points next week.
JAKARTA - Jakarta stocks are seen steady next week following a strong set of first quarter corporate earnings, brokers said.
"More foreign players are likely to re-enter the market which should keep sentiment firm especially after announcements of strong first quarter results," one broker said.
Brokers also said Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad's comment that the government planned to merge state banks were also likely to keep sentiment firm on the banking sector.
On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed 3.4 points or 0.49 percent stronger at 698.62 against last week's close of 695.02.

BANGKOK - Thai stocks are seen flat with a weak tone in the coming week on lack of foreign investor interest following a central bank move to curb foreign baht funding through the stock market, brokers said.
"Foreign trading activities would remain thin. Without their buying, I don't think the market will move much," Songklod Bhichaikul, an analyst at United Securities, said.
Worries about weak bank earnings and rising low-quality assets will also dampen local sentiment.
The market is seen testing the 500 support level next week.
The composite index closed 4.16 points lower at a new 97-month low of 515.60 on Friday. Week-on-week, the key index fell 18.86 points from the previous week's level of 534.46.
MANILA - Philippine shares are seen struggling higher next week with buying in issues expected to post improved profits for the second quarter of the year, traders said.

"We see the market a little on the upside with companies seasonally performing well during the second quarter being bought ahead of the release of second quarter earnings results," said Mayenne Catimbang at Magnum International Securities. The market is seen testing initial resistance at 2,820.

The main index closed 13.87 points higher on Friday at 2,801.61, breaching the 2800 resistance. Week-on-week, the main index rose 38.81 points or 1.40 percent from the previous level of 2,762.80 points.
SEOUL - Seoul stocks are expected to rise next week on active buying backed by the ample liquidity, and construction and securities firms are likely to lead gains, analysts said.

"I see the market's sentiment remaining bullish throughout the week in view of the continued high liquidity," said Yi Seung-gook, head of research at the Seoul branch of ABN AMRO Hoare Govett Asia Ltd.
Cash liquidity has been high because financial insitutions tightened credit offerings to companies since they saw a string of corporate collapses this year, analysts said.
The composite index closed at 791.97 on Saturday, up 3.8 percent or 29.2 points from last Saturday's 762.77.
SINGAPORE - Weaker-than-expected corporate results and a lacklustre Singapore economy are weighing down the stock market as foreign funds sell, dealers said.
"Micro and macro factors don't look good. Fund managers continue to downgrade Singapore, especially after the unpleasant earning surprises of heavyweight blue chips," said a dealer.
The key Straits Times Industrials Index ended down 0.56 points, at 1,990.12 on Friday compared to 2,032.30 a week ago.
The index is expected to drift to around 1,900 by the end of June, some dealers said.
KUALA LUMPUR - Malaysian stocks will trade

cautiously next week with investors worried about spillover from continuing problems in neighbouring Thailand, brokers said. Malaysia has lately been plagued by lack of foreign fund support amid the high interest rate scenario.
Analysts said though some big capitalised issues look attractive, buying interest is low.

For the week, the Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks closed 38.93 points or 3.48 percent lower from Friday a week ago. On Friday the index fell 22.03 points or two percent to 1,078.38 from Thursday's close.
SYDNEY - Australian investors are seen watching Wall Street closely next week with the lack of local corporate news also helping to drive the rumour mill.
The All Ordinaries index capped a strong week with a 17.2 point gain on Friday. The index added 54.4 points or 2.1 percent for the week and closed at a record high at 2,655.3.

"I'm suprised Wall Street hasn't had more down days lately. It will make local investors more cautious - too many people remember October 1987," said Grant Williams, a dealer at Sydney brokerage Reynolds & Co.
WELLINGTON - New Zealand shares ended weaker on
Friday and brokers expect the market next week to continue on a volatile track but with limited upside.
Domestic investors were continuing to ignore Wall Street's string of record gains, as has been the case for several months.
Paul Nicolson at SBC Warburg said Friday's decline came as orders petered out.
"It's just a case of our market having a reasonable run in the last little while and it feels pretty close to fair value relative to bond prices," he said.
"So in spite of the Dow continuing to run hard, there does not appear to be too much steam in our market at this stage."
The NZSE-40 Capital Index closed the week at 2,366.29, up just 9.49 points or 0.4 percent on last Friday.
